findings.description: publicly_accessible = true assigns the RDS instance a public endpoint reachable from the internet, exposing the MySQL service to internet-wide scanning and credential attacks even though the database serves only an internal EC2 web tier that should reach it privately.

storage_encrypted = false leaves the RDS volumes, snapshots and automated backups unencrypted, so any access to the underlying storage or a shared snapshot yields cleartext data. No KMS customer-managed key is configured either.

The master user is the default name "admin", which removes any need for an attacker to guess the privileged username and makes brute-force attacks against the publicly reachable endpoint substantially easier.

The custom parameter group applied to this instance does not set require_secure_transport (or equivalent TLS enforcement), so the database accepts unencrypted client connections; combined with a public endpoint, credentials and query data can traverse the network in cleartext.

No enabled_cloudwatch_logs_exports (audit, error, general, slowquery) and no IAM database authentication are configured, so authentication and query activity against this internet-facing database leaves no durable audit trail for security investigation.

The user_data script interpolates var.password and the DB username directly into a shell heredoc, so the database master credentials are stored in EC2 instance metadata and are readable by anyone with ec2:DescribeInstanceAttribute or from the instance metadata service itself.

No metadata_options block sets http_tokens = "required", so the legacy unauthenticated IMDSv1 remains enabled. A server-side request forgery in the PHP application would let an attacker retrieve the instance profile's credentials, which in this configuration grant near-administrative S3/EC2/RDS access.
No root_block_device with encrypted = true is specified, so the instance's root volume — which holds the dbinfo.inc file containing the database password — is written to unencrypted storage.

The inline policy grants s3:*, ec2:* and rds:* on Resource "*", which is effectively administrative over data, compute and databases in the account. Combined with the EC2 instance profile and IMDSv1, a single application compromise becomes full account-level data access and a privilege-escalation path (ec2:* permits RunInstances/PassRole style escalation).

Egress allows all protocols and ports to 0.0.0.0/0 from the RDS security group, providing an unrestricted data-exfiltration and command-and-control channel rather than limiting outbound traffic to what the workload requires.
